heatwave = a period of unusually hot weather lasting several days
drought = a long period with far too little rain
precipitation = rain, snow, sleet or hail that falls from the sky
humidity = the amount of water vapour in the air
torrential rain = extremely heavy rain that falls very fast
downpour = a sudden, heavy fall of rain
unseasonable weather = weather that is unusual for that time of year
mild winter = a winter that is warmer than usual
temperate climate = a climate that is neither extremely hot nor extremely cold
arid climate = a climate with very little rainfall
microclimate = the distinctive climate of a small area
prevailing wind = the wind that most often blows in a particular region
atmospheric pressure = the weight of the air pressing down on the Earth
climate change = long-term shifts in temperature and weather patterns, largely caused by human activity
global warming = the rise in the Earth's average temperature
greenhouse effect = the way certain gases trap heat in the atmosphere
greenhouse gas = a gas such as carbon dioxide that traps heat in the atmosphere
carbon dioxide = a greenhouse gas produced by burning fossil fuels and by breathing
carbon footprint = the amount of greenhouse gas produced by a person, product or activity
ecological footprint = the amount of land and resources needed to support a lifestyle
ozone layer = a layer of gas in the upper atmosphere that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays
ozone depletion = the thinning of the ozone layer caused by certain chemicals
climate crisis = the urgent, large-scale threat posed by rapid climate change
extreme weather = weather that is unusually severe, such as violent storms or record heat
sea-level rise = the increase in the height of the world's oceans
ice cap = a thick layer of ice covering a large area, especially at the poles
glacier = a huge, slow-moving mass of ice in mountains or polar regions
permafrost = ground that stays frozen all year in polar regions
desertification = the process by which fertile land becomes dry and desert-like
monsoon = a seasonal wind that brings heavy rain, especially in South Asia
smog = dirty air caused by smoke, exhaust fumes and fog mixing
acid rain = rain made acidic by pollution, which damages forests and lakes
coastline = the edge of the land where it meets the sea
wetland = land that is covered with water for much of the year
marshland = low, wet land that is often flooded
peat bog = a wet area of land made of decaying plants, used as a carbon store
estuary = the wide tidal mouth of a river where it meets the sea
river delta = flat land formed where a river splits into branches before the sea
tributary = a smaller river that flows into a larger one
floodplain = flat land beside a river that floods in heavy rain
groundwater = water stored under the ground in soil and rock
aquifer = an underground layer of rock that holds water
fertile soil = soil that is rich in nutrients and good for growing crops
soil erosion = the wearing away of topsoil by wind or water
weathering = the slow breaking down of rock by weather, water or plants
coral reef = an underwater structure built by corals, rich in marine life
mangrove forest = trees that grow in salty coastal water and protect the shore
tundra = a cold, treeless region with a short growing season
savannah = a grassy plain with scattered trees in a hot climate
woodland = land covered with trees, often smaller than a forest
forest canopy = the upper layer of leaves and branches in a forest
undergrowth = bushes and plants growing beneath the trees
peninsula = a piece of land almost surrounded by water
archipelago = a group of islands
plateau = a large area of high, fairly flat land
terrain = the physical features of an area of land
endangered species = a type of animal or plant at serious risk of dying out
habitat = the natural environment where a plant or animal lives
predator = an animal that hunts and kills other animals for food
prey = an animal that is hunted by another animal
food chain = a series of living things in which each is eaten by the next
ecosystem = a community of living things and their physical environment
biodiversity = the variety of plant and animal species in an area
flora = the plants of a particular region or period
fauna = the animals of a particular region or period
mammal = a warm-blooded animal that feeds its young on milk
amphibian = an animal such as a frog that lives both in water and on land
reptile = a cold-blooded animal such as a snake, lizard or turtle
invertebrate = an animal without a backbone, such as an insect or worm
pollinator = an animal, often an insect, that carries pollen from one flower to another
scavenger = an animal that feeds on dead animals or waste
herbivore = an animal that eats only plants
carnivore = an animal that eats other animals
apex predator = a predator at the top of the food chain, with no natural enemies
keystone species = a species whose presence keeps a whole ecosystem in balance
invasive species = a plant or animal brought in from elsewhere that harms local wildlife
native species = a plant or animal that naturally belongs in a particular place
extinction = the complete disappearance of a species from the Earth
critically endangered = at extremely high risk of extinction in the wild
breeding ground = a place where animals regularly gather to produce young
wildlife corridor = a strip of habitat that lets animals move safely between areas
habitat loss = the destruction of the natural places where species live
habitat fragmentation = the splitting of a habitat into smaller, isolated pieces
overfishing = catching so many fish that stocks cannot recover
poaching = the illegal hunting or catching of wild animals
wildlife trafficking = the illegal trade in wild animals or their body parts
captive breeding = breeding endangered animals in zoos or centres to save the species
camouflage = colouring or shape that helps an animal hide in its surroundings
adaptation = a feature that helps a living thing survive in its environment
hibernation = a long, deep sleep through winter to save energy
migration = the regular, long-distance movement of animals, usually seasonally
vegetation = the plants growing in a particular area
deciduous forest = a forest of trees that shed their leaves in autumn
evergreen = a plant that keeps its leaves all year
decomposer = an organism that breaks down dead plants and animals
genetic diversity = variety in the genes of a species, which helps it survive change
earthquake = a sudden, violent shaking of the ground
flood = water covering land that is normally dry
wildfire = a large, uncontrolled fire in countryside or forest
landslide = a sudden fall of rock or earth down a slope
avalanche = a large mass of snow falling rapidly down a mountain
tsunami = a huge sea wave caused by an underwater earthquake or eruption
volcanic eruption = when a volcano throws out lava, ash and gas
hurricane = a very powerful tropical storm with extremely strong winds
tornado = a violent, spinning column of air that touches the ground
cyclone = a large, rotating storm system, often over tropical seas
aftershock = a smaller earthquake that follows a larger one
epicentre = the point on the Earth's surface above where an earthquake starts
magnitude = a number that measures the strength of an earthquake
seismic activity = earthquakes and other vibrations in the Earth's crust
flash flood = a sudden flood after extremely heavy rain
storm surge = a rise in sea level driven onshore by a storm
mudslide = a rapid flow of wet earth down a slope
natural disaster = a sudden natural event that causes serious damage and loss of life
evacuate = to move people from a dangerous place to safety
early-warning system = technology and procedures that alert people before a disaster hits
disaster relief = practical help given after a flood, quake or similar event
flood defences = walls, barriers and other structures built to keep floodwater out
famine = an extreme shortage of food affecting a whole region
crop failure = a situation in which harvests are much smaller than expected
deforestation = the large-scale cutting down of forests
pollution = harmful substances that make air, water or land dirty
recycling = processing used materials so they can be made into new products
landfill = a site where rubbish is buried in the ground
fossil fuels = coal, oil and gas formed from ancient plants and animals
renewable energy = power from sources that will not run out, such as wind or sun
sustainability = using resources in a way that does not damage the future
conservation = the protection of animals, plants and natural places
carbon emissions = the release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
exhaust fumes = gases produced by engines, especially in vehicles
air quality = how clean or polluted the air is in a place
water contamination = the presence of harmful substances in water
industrial waste = unwanted material produced by factories and industry
toxic waste = rubbish that is poisonous and dangerous to living things
sewage = waste water from homes and toilets
incineration = the burning of waste at high temperatures
single-use plastic = plastic items designed to be thrown away after one use
biodegradable = able to be broken down naturally by bacteria or fungi
composting = turning kitchen and garden waste into soil improver
solar power = electricity generated from sunlight
wind farm = a group of wind turbines that generate electricity
hydropower = electricity generated from moving water
geothermal energy = heat from inside the Earth used to make power or warm buildings
nuclear power = electricity produced by splitting atoms in a reactor
oil spill = an accidental release of oil into the sea or onto land
fracking = extracting gas or oil by injecting liquid into rock at high pressure
overgrazing = allowing too many animals to feed on land, so plants cannot recover
sustainable development = economic progress that does not destroy the environment or future resources
eco-friendly = designed to cause little harm to the environment
greenwashing = making a product or company look more environmentally friendly than it is
carbon-neutral = balancing the carbon you produce by saving the same amount elsewhere
net zero = cutting emissions and offsetting the rest so the total is zero
reforestation = planting trees again where forest has been cut down
afforestation = planting trees on land that was not recently forest
rewilding = restoring land so that natural processes and wildlife can return
nature reserve = an area of land protected for wildlife and habitats
marine protected area = a part of the sea where fishing and other damage are limited
conservationist = a person who works to protect animals, plants and habitats
environmentalist = a person who campaigns to protect the natural environment
Paris Agreement = the 2015 international treaty to limit global warming
methane = a powerful greenhouse gas produced by livestock, waste and leaks
energy efficiency = using less energy to do the same job
fly-tipping = illegally dumping rubbish in the countryside or on waste ground
waste sorting = separating rubbish into types such as paper, glass and bio-waste
circular economy = an economic model that reuses and recycles instead of throwing away
finite resources = materials that will eventually run out
deplete = to reduce something until little remains
water scarcity = a serious shortage of fresh water
pesticide = a chemical used to kill insects that damage crops
fertiliser = a substance added to soil to help plants grow
intensive farming = producing as much food as possible from the land, often with chemicals
organic farming = growing food without most synthetic chemicals
monoculture = growing only one crop over a large area
soil degradation = the decline in soil quality so that it grows less food
irrigation = supplying water to land so that crops can grow
microplastics = tiny pieces of plastic that pollute soil, water and living things
ocean acidification = the sea becoming more acidic as it absorbs extra carbon dioxide
coral bleaching = corals turning white and often dying when seas become too warm
illegal logging = cutting down trees in breach of the law
slash-and-burn = clearing land by cutting and burning vegetation, often for farming
